issues.description: The manuscript states that all included replications met a minimum sample size of 120, yet the reported sample sizes include 80, 81, 90, 94, and 116. This contradiction undermines confidence in the inclusion criteria, preregistration adherence, and power claims.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.description: Most individual replications had small samples relative to the original effects being tested, and several had approximately the original sample size rather than a substantially larger replication sample. This limits power to detect small-to-moderate correlations and makes individual nonsignificant findings difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: no adequate sample-size planning for precision
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that their design was not planned for accuracy in parameter estimation. Because replication conclusions depend heavily on effect-size precision and effect-size comparisons, inadequate planning reduces the evidential value of both individual studies and the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: fully committing to goal (3) would require a different form of sample size planning (accuracy in parameter estimation; see Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

issues.description: The OSF project had 17 forks, but only seven studies were included because they posted data/results and met criteria. The manuscript does not explain the status of the other 10 forks, whether they collected data, or whether their exclusion could bias the meta-analysis. This is especially important because incomplete or unreported replications can function like a file drawer.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks” representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository. All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.description: All samples were undergraduate students at U.S. colleges/universities, yet the introduction frames the topic in terms of Facebook’s global user base. Findings from convenience samples of undergraduates cannot be generalized to Facebook users broadly without qualification.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted

issues.description: The manuscript does not state that participants were required to be active Facebook users. If participants did not use Facebook or used it minimally, their perceptions of Facebook self-disclosure, expression, and connection may be uninformed or qualitatively different, threatening construct validity.
issues.quote: Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012).

issues.description: The original study was published in 2012, whereas replications were conducted in 2016–2017 after substantial changes in social media use and the rise of Instagram/Snapchat. This threatens the assumption that the replication context is equivalent to the original, yet platform-use changes were not measured or modeled.
issues.quote: the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.description: Studies differed in whether participants completed measures in the lab, online, or both. Mode of administration can affect privacy, attention, social desirability, and responses to self-disclosure items. These differences were not standardized or analyzed as moderators.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods).

issues.description: One replication tested participants in groups, unlike other replications where lab participants completed questionnaires alone. Group testing may alter privacy concerns and responses to items about disclosure and interpersonal safety.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: One replication changed item wording and item order for the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale. Even apparently minor changes can affect scale validity and comparability, especially for a replication that hinges on the self-esteem predictor.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., ‘At times I think I am no good at all’ vs. ‘I think I am no good at all’)

issues.description: Two replications used a five-point Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale while others used a four-point scale. This may alter distributions, reliability, and comparability across studies, yet it was not modeled or justified.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.description: The manuscript indicates that some studies used mean scores while at least one appeared to use summed scores. Although correlations may be invariant to linear transformations, inconsistent scoring complicates descriptive comparisons, missing-data handling, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: The authors did not have analysis scripts or narratives for all studies and therefore could not determine key analytic decisions such as missing-data handling, exclusions, or composite construction. This directly limits reproducibility and makes the meta-analyzed effects difficult to verify.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.description: The manuscript notes that data were not consistently collected or stored, including item-level data. Without item-level data, researchers cannot verify reverse coding, reliability, missingness, or scoring decisions.
issues.quote: Data were not always collected or stored consistently (e.g., race collected in some but not all studies; individual item-level data were not always stored).

issues.description: Although datasets were available, the authors appear to have relied on each team’s independently conducted analyses except when one study lacked regression results. This allows site-specific scoring, exclusions, and missing-data choices to propagate into the meta-analysis rather than applying one harmonized analytic pipeline.
issues.quote: After completion of data collection, teams independently analyzed the results and posted their materials, data, and results on their project’s OSF pages.

issues.subcategory: unclear or possibly incorrect meta-analytic variance handling
issues.description: The manuscript says the metafor rma function accepted effect size r and N parameters, but rma requires effect estimates and sampling variances or appropriate transformed inputs. The manuscript does not report Fisher z transformation or the variance formula used for correlations. If raw r values and sample sizes were used incorrectly, meta-analytic estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, and prediction intervals may be invalid; even if the code was correct, the reporting is insufficient for replication.
issues.quote: The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters

issues.subcategory: failure to report Fisher z transformation
issues.description: Correlations are typically meta-analyzed after Fisher z transformation because the sampling distribution of r is skewed and its variance depends on the true correlation. The manuscript does not state that this was done, creating uncertainty about the validity of the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables

issues.description: The authors compared REML and DerSimonian-Laird and selected REML because it produced “more interpretable” heterogeneity estimates. Choosing a statistical model based on interpretability of results rather than a prespecified rationale can introduce analytic flexibility. REML is defensible, but the selection rationale is weak.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.description: The seven replications came from five institutions, with multiple studies from the same institutions and teams. Treating all effects as fully independent may underestimate uncertainty if site, investigator, or participant-pool characteristics induce dependence.
issues.quote: These CREP research teams represented five diverse institutions

issues.subcategory: small number of studies for random-effects meta-analysis
issues.description: A random-effects meta-analysis with only seven studies yields imprecise heterogeneity estimates, unreliable prediction intervals, and limited ability to detect moderators. The authors acknowledge this but still interpret heterogeneity, prediction intervals, and fail-safe numbers substantively.
issues.quote: Seven studies provide important data about the replicability of a finding, but severely limit the inferences we feel confident to draw from the data.

issues.description: The manuscript interprets prediction intervals as showing what 95% of future studies would find. With only seven studies and imprecise tau estimates, such statements are overconfident. Prediction intervals describe model-based uncertainty, not guaranteed future-study outcomes.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.subcategory: incorrect or inconsistent prediction interval reporting
issues.description: For self-disclosure safety, the results report a prediction interval of [-.54, -.03], but the discussion reports [-.40, -.15], which is the confidence interval reported in the results rather than the prediction interval. This confuses uncertainty about the mean effect with expected variation across future studies.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was -.28, 95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03], p < .001.

issues.subcategory: confidence interval mistaken for prediction interval
issues.description: The discussion states that the 95% PI for self-disclosure safety is [-.40, -.15], but this interval was reported earlier as the confidence interval. This is a substantive reporting error because CIs and PIs answer different questions.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.description: Fail-safe N is a limited and often discouraged publication-bias metric, especially with very small meta-analyses and preregistered replications. The manuscript uses FSN as evidence of robustness and as a basis for confidence about future findings, which is not warranted.
issues.quote: These results also seemed to be somewhat robust, as indicated by a high FSN (133).

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N applied to nonsignificant result
issues.description: The manuscript reports a fail-safe number for the connection outcome even though the meta-analytic result was nonsignificant. FSN is defined by the authors as the number of null studies needed to reduce a significant result to nonsignificance, so its use for a nonsignificant result is conceptually unclear.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065... The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.description: The manuscript gives different FSN values for the same outcomes in the results and discussion, reducing confidence in the analyses and interpretation.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies.

issues.description: The discussion states that five unreported studies would reduce the expression result to nonsignificance, whereas the results section reports FSN = 3. This inconsistency affects interpretation of robustness.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant

issues.description: For connection, the results report FSN = 5, but the discussion states FSN = 11. The discrepancy indicates either a reporting error or unstable/incorrect analyses.
issues.quote: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.description: The manuscript infers publication bias in the original study from smaller replication effects and a prediction interval. Publication bias cannot be established from one original study and seven replications without an appropriate bias model or broader evidence about the literature.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study.

issues.description: The manuscript suggests that an original p-value of .05 is evidence against the original effect because p-values between .04 and .05 are more likely under the null. This inference depends on assumptions about power, selection, and p-value distributions and is not a valid basis for evaluating a single study’s result.
issues.quote: p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: nonsignificance interpreted as evidence of no effect
issues.description: The authors repeatedly interpret nonsignificant individual regressions or CIs including zero as evidence that self-esteem does not relate to expression. Without equivalence testing, Bayes factors, or sufficiently narrow intervals, nonsignificance does not establish absence of an effect.
issues.quote: Self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).

issues.description: For opportunity to express self, the meta-analysis found a statistically significant positive effect, yet the manuscript concludes that the replications support the original nonsignificant finding. This is internally inconsistent and reflects overreliance on individual-study nonsignificance.
issues.quote: the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero

issues.description: The results report p = .065 for the connection meta-analysis, but the discussion says the meta-analytic effect was significantly different from zero. This is a direct statistical contradiction.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065.

issues.description: The discussion incorrectly describes the connection meta-analytic effect as significant despite the reported p = .065 and confidence interval including zero.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent original effect size for advantageous disclosure
issues.description: The original effect size for advantageous disclosure is reported inconsistently as -.30, -.33, and beta = -.300. Inconsistent reporting makes comparisons between original and replication effects unclear.
issues.quote: Self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent original effect size for advantageous disclosure
issues.description: Table 3 uses original r = -.33 for advantageous disclosure, while the abstract and Table 1 report -.30. The manuscript does not explain the discrepancy between standardized beta and effect size r.

issues.subcategory: unclear sign convention for effect-size differences
issues.description: Table 3 labels a column “Difference” but does not define whether it is original minus replication or replication minus original. Several signs are opposite what readers would expect from replication minus original, creating interpretive ambiguity.
issues.quote: Study | Replication r | Original r | Difference | 95% CI

issues.description: For connection, most replication effects were positive while the original was negative. Describing these effects as “smaller” is ambiguous or misleading because they are opposite in direction rather than merely smaller in magnitude.
issues.quote: five of the seven replications had effect sizes significantly smaller from the original study

issues.description: The manuscript evaluates four outcomes, seven individual regressions per outcome, multiple effect-size difference tests, and several meta-analytic tests without discussing multiplicity or preregistered prioritization. This increases the chance of false-positive interpretations, especially for marginal effects.
issues.quote: For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions.

issues.description: The manuscript often treats effect-size difference confidence intervals that include zero as indicating similarity to the original. Wide CIs can reflect low precision rather than equivalence; equivalence tests or predefined smallest-effect thresholds would be needed to support similarity.
issues.quote: six of the seven replications had effect size differences from the original that were not significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The results frequently summarize replication success by counting how many individual p-values were significant. Vote-counting is statistically inefficient and can be misleading because it ignores effect-size precision and power differences across studies.
issues.quote: five of the seven replications found self-esteem to be a significant predictor

issues.description: With only seven studies and one much larger study, conclusions may depend strongly on individual studies. The manuscript does not report leave-one-out analyses, influence diagnostics, or sensitivity to excluding methodologically divergent studies.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.description: The Facebook perception measures were created by the original researchers and are described mainly by internal consistency. The manuscript does not provide evidence of factorial validity, measurement invariance across sites, or stability over time, which matters when comparing samples and historical contexts.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012).

issues.description: The connection subscale had reliability as low as alpha = .68 in some datasets. Lower reliability attenuates correlations and may partly explain weak or inconsistent effects, but this is not examined.
issues.quote: connection: .68 to .84

issues.subcategory: perceived benefits conflated with actual benefits
issues.description: The measures assess perceptions of safety, advantages, expression, and connection, not actual self-disclosure behavior, social outcomes, or benefits. Some interpretations imply real-world benefits or improved social relations, which the data cannot establish.
issues.quote: those with low self-esteem perceived benefits for self-disclosure through Facebook compared to face-to-face interactions

issues.description: The studies are cross-sectional and correlational, yet the manuscript repeatedly uses “predictor” language and draws implications about self-esteem leading to perceptions. Regression prediction does not establish causal direction.
issues.quote: self-esteem was a significant predictor of perceiving Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose than FTF

issues.description: The manuscript claims support for social compensation theory, but the studies measured perceived safety/advantages, not actual compensation, anxiety reduction, Facebook use for compensation, or social outcomes. The theoretical inference is therefore indirect.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory

issues.description: Race was collected in only three replications and other demographic variables were not collected. This prevents evaluation of sample comparability, demographic moderation, and generalizability, especially given known demographic differences in social media use.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected

issues.description: The samples were predominantly female, and the manuscript does not test or adjust for gender differences. If self-esteem or Facebook perceptions differ by gender, this may affect estimated associations and generalizability.
issues.quote: Across datasets, 67% of all participants were female and 33% were male

issues.description: The manuscript states that individual studies were preregistered but does not describe preregistered hypotheses, exclusion rules, missing-data handling, scoring rules, or deviations. This limits the value of the preregistration claim for evaluating analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: After receiving approval of the replication materials and procedure, contributors pre-registered their studies before data collection.

issues.description: Although individual studies were preregistered, the manuscript does not state that the meta-analysis inclusion criteria, extraction rules, transformations, estimator choice, or sensitivity analyses were preregistered. This leaves room for post hoc analytic decisions.
issues.quote: This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page

issues.description: The authors identify multiple procedural differences across studies but do not analyze them. Even if underpowered, these differences complicate claims of direct replication and may explain heterogeneity or effect reversals.
issues.quote: we know there are methodological and procedural differences between the studies (i.e., in-person vs. online; individual participants vs. groups; wording on questionnaires; additional measures). Because each of these potential moderating factors occurred in only one or two of the seven replications, we chose not to explore these issues in more depth.

issues.description: Tables as presented contain duplicated headings and repeated confidence interval columns, which impairs clarity and increases risk of misreading results.
issues.quote: Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous

issues.description: The original study did not report the beta coefficient for expression, yet the manuscript uses an original r = .15 in Table 3. The derivation and sign of this effect should be explicitly documented because it is used in replication comparisons.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.

issues.subcategory: direct replication claim weakened by deviations
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly labels the studies direct replications, but documented deviations in administration mode, group versus individual testing, item wording, response scales, scoring, and additional measures weaken that claim. This matters because conclusions are framed as direct evidence about replicability of the original study.
issues.quote: All studies reported in this research were direct replications of the original.
